about: The words of the chain house_debt (Data/encounters/chain_house_debt_793.json; the page is Design/content/chains/house_debt.md): the 1,920 pennies (480 until 7 Oct 2026) owed to the count of Dorestad, written 4 Oct 2026. Keys are chain_house_debt.<step>.<what>; the two news_ keys are items for Dorestad's board; art.<card id> is one line for the artist on each card's picture. Nothing here is quoted from a book: the king's man's line on traders follows Charles's letter to Offa of 796 in our own words. A draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The tally

The count's steward waits at the dam head with a hazel stick split down its length. His half and yours say the same thing: eight pounds of silver, 1,920 pennies, lent for the boat and due at Michaelmas.
Forty dozen pennies. I cut the notches myself the day the boat was paid for, and I cut them deep. Hold your half against mine. They fit now, and they will fit at Michaelmas.
The count is away with the host. He is home for Michaelmas, and that is the day. I do not move days.
Michaelmas has gone by. The count asks after you every court day, and every court day I tell him the river is long.
He asks back what he lent and not a penny over it. The king forbids more, and so does the Church. So do not be late. A day has no price, and that is what makes it dear.
You are known on the dams, so I will say this once. His people are short of bread-corn, and he wants a hawk from the north to give the king. A man who brought either would find him easier to talk to.
Take your half and say you will be there
Leave twelve pennies for the count's table, as the custom is
Say the boat was never worth eight pounds
A friend on the bank road

Thiadbod, who has the best dam head in Dorestat and a gift for every officer, comes along the bank road in a blue cloak to wish you well. His sister, the widow Thiadburg, watches from her storehouse door.
Two pounds by Michaelmas, in that? I have casks that weigh more than your boat. Still, I began small myself. Smaller than I tell people.
I want six bolts of English cloth, and my own ship is bound up the Rhine. Bring them inside two moons and I pay well over the dam's price. Friends should help each other to their days.
The count eats at my table when he is home. I will say your name to him. Kindly.
My brother gives nothing he has not counted twice. Ask him whose hazel sticks hang in his storehouse. Sibrad had a boat of his own once. He rows my brother's now.
And ask yourself why he sends you to the English for it, when their reeves turn Frankish keels away, and his own ship has not left her post since Easter.
If you are short when the day comes, come to me before you go to him. I lend on goods I can see, and what I am lent I give back.
Take his order for English cloth
Thank him and take no favours
Ask him, before his sister, whose sticks hang in his storehouse
The count's day
The reckoning. In the count's hall the steward lays the two halves of the hazel stick together on the board, and the count looks at you over them.
The halves fit. Forty dozen. Nothing has been cut off.
You are here for the day, shipman. Most are not.
Michaelmas is long past, shipman. I looked for you and saw only my steward's face, which I see every day.
My steward says you left twelve pennies for my table at midsummer. I ate them. They were good.
A count and his whole following were cut down on the Weser this year, and the king has turned back from the Avars for it. I am in no mood for stories. Silver, or what you have in its place.
I ask back what I lent. The king forbids me more and I want no more. But a broken day is a debt of another kind, and that one I may collect as I please.
And hear this, whatever you pay. My people have eaten their seed. Bring wheat up the river before the frost and my steward pays a fair price for it. That is not a favour I ask. It is one I offer.
And if you are ever in the north: he wants a hawk for the king's fist. He has said so every day since Easter.
Count out what you still owe, on the day
Count out what you still owe, late
Ask until next Michaelmas, and offer the boat's work for it
Lay the mooring rope on the board: the boat is his pledge
The hungry winter
The count's steward stands on the bank with a list of the households on the count's land that have eaten their seed corn. He looks into every hold that comes up the river.
Nine score mouths on the count's land, and bread for half of them. What is under your boards?
There was ice in the ditches between the dams this morning. After this the river brings nothing till Easter.
The count pays six pennies the sack for wheat, counted here. On the dams they will give you twelve and bless you for it. I know it. So does he.
That is wheat. I can smell wheat through oak.
No wheat under there. A man cannot eat millstones, though I have seen it tried this year.
You offered the boat's work for your year. This is the work.
They come to the church door at first light and I have nothing to break for them. A sack given there is lent to a lord who has never missed a day.
One thing more, from the count. A man who pays his day can be trusted with stores. When the grass is up the host goes east, and he wants hulls at Daventre. He pays a penny a load.
Sell the count four sacks at his price
Sell four sacks on the dams at the hungry price
Carry two sacks to the church door and sell him the other two
You have no corn to spare
The king's new penny

The mint at Dorestat is striking the king's new penny, broad and heavy, with his name tied in a knot of letters. The count has heard the law from Frankfurt read, and has sent for every man whose stick still hangs in his hall.
Old penny. New penny. Four of the new weigh five of the old and a little over. The fire does not care whose name is on them.
The king says there is one penny now, and a free man who refuses it pays fifteen shillings. So a penny is this. Your stick says pennies, forty dozen of them.
By tale, then. What is cut on the stick, counted out in the new coin.
What he lent was weighed in the old pound. I weighed it. Eighteen score and seven of the new pennies is that weight again. Give him the tale and he has near a third more silver than left his hand.
Do not say the word you are about to say, moneyer. I have asked for pennies. I have asked for nothing the king forbids.
This one sold us wheat at the count's price when the dams paid double. It is on my sticks, so I say it.
And his mooring rope has hung on my wall since the reckoning.
Pay what you owe by tale in the new pennies, and see the stick burned
Have the moneyer weigh out what you owe in new pennies, about three for every four by tale, and pay that
Say you will answer at Michaelmas
The stick for sale

The count is making ready to ride with the host, and he does not mean to leave an open stick behind him. Thiadbod stands at his elbow in a clean blue cloak. On the board lie your tally, a purse and a cask of wine.
The king goes into Saxony after the harvest with two armies, and I go with one. I will not carry a hazel stick to the Saxons.
I ride with the host again, shipman, and your stick has hung a year too long.
Thiadbod offers me forty dozen of the new pennies for it, and a cask for my trouble. A man may sell what is owed him. Match it, or give me a reason.
So the bishop sent you home with a blessing. Blessings take no notches off a stick.
I told you I would say your name to the count. Kindly.
You carried my cloth well. You will carry my wine better.
Six score pennies in my hand now and a third of your next three cargoes, and I pay the count myself. My brother can drink his own cask.
I lend to people who listen. I spoke to you once on the bank road, and you did not.
If you mean to say usury, say it at Traiectum, to the man whose word it is. Not in this hall.
Match the bid: what you owe, in new pennies, and the stick is burned
Take the widow's surety: a quarter of the debt now and a third of three cargoes
Say the bishop will hear of it, and go down to Traiectum
Let him sell it
Saint Martin's man

Inside the old stone fort at Traiectum the bishop hears you between the hours, a deacon with a book beside him. He has waited a long time for a complaint against the count of Dorestat that he could put in writing.
The count of Dorestat and I share a river and nothing else. Sit. Tell it from the day the stick was cut.

To ask back more than was lent is usury. It is forbidden to every Christian, clerk and layman alike, and the king has had it written so. I can write it again, to the count, in a hand he will need a priest to read to him.
A letter holds him to the weight and no more. You would still owe the weight, and you would pay it here, to my clerk, who carries it up the river with the letter. Eighteen score and seven.

Or there is a shorter road. The men of Saint Martin who live on his banks at Dorestat owe the king's officers nothing: no toll, no lodging, no hand on their goods when they die. And Saint Martin has silver enough to buy one hazel stick.

But a man is not a stick. Saint Martin's man carries wax and wine when he is asked, and answers in my hall, not the count's. Think before you kneel. I would rather have a willing boatman than a sorry one.
Kneel, and put your hands between his
Ask for the letter and pay the debt by weight to his clerk
Thank him and go back up the river as you came
Stores for the host
Carts and horse lines on the river bank at Daventre, and one of the count's men counting sacks on a wax tablet. The host goes east into Saxony again, and its stores must cross the river and go up it.
The Dorestat shipman. The count said a small boat that pays her days might come. I did not believe him.
Meal, salt pork and horse-corn, over the river and up the brook as far as she floats. Twelve days of it. The count pays a penny a load, and he pays.
Two armies this year, they say, one from each side, and the Saxons between them like corn between stones.
The king means to be on the Elbe before harvest, they say, and to bring home more hostages than in any year yet.
This year it is ships. Great ones, hauled over dry land like sledges to reach the Saxon rivers. I have seen it and I still do not believe it.
Every year I say it is the last year, and every year the Saxons make a liar of me.
I will not lie to you. If the water falls she stays where she lies until it rises, and the host does not wait to pay.
And if you ever go north, bring the count a hawk. He wants one for the king's fist more than he wants his dinner.
Carry the stores for twelve days
Take his order for salt pork instead
Say the boat has her own summer
A hawk from the north
The count has come down to the dam head himself, which he does not do. Somebody has told him what sits on the perch in your stern.
Take the cloth off her. Slowly. I want to see her before she sees me.
He has not looked at a tally like that in twenty years.
The king hunts from the leaf-fall to Christmas. A count who sets that on the king's fist is asked to sit nearer the fire, and he does not forget who set it on his own.
You paid me on the day, and now this. One day you may want something only a king can give. Ask me then. I will carry the asking.
The dam's price for a hawk like that is ten score pennies. He knows it. He is hoping you will not say it.
Give him the hawk for the king
Sell him the hawk at the dam's price
Keep her for another market
The king's man
Strangers sit at the count's own board, sent to take every free man's oath and to hear any man's wrong. The count stands by the door of his own hall, and every tally stick in it lies on the board.
By the lord king's order every man from twelve years up swears to be faithful to him, and I write the names. After that I hear what any man has to say against any other, count or cowherd.

By the lord emperor's order every man from twelve years up swears to him by name, as a man ought to his lord, and the names are written. After that we hear any man's wrong against any other, count or cowherd.
The lord Charles wrote it to King Offa of the English himself: traders have his protection, and one who suffers wrongful oppression may appeal to him or to his judges. I am one of his judges.
A vassal from the palace with one good horse and a thin cloak. Men like that have been known to ride home with two horses.
An abbot and a count from far up the Rhine, with land enough of their own. The emperor chose such men, they say, because they have no need of gifts.
This is the shipman I spoke of. Ask him what kind of lord I am. I will stand outside while he says it.
Say what you like, shipman. I know who came when I called and who did not.
Some of these sticks the count cut. Some, I am told, hang now in a merchant's storehouse, and went there for a cask of wine. I would like to hear about those from a man who has held one.
Say the count dealt justly with you
Tell him how sticks are sold in this hall
Tell the emperor's envoys how sticks are sold in this hall
A hen at Michaelmas
The king's man has ridden on. The count sends for you, not to the hall but to the bank below it, where a strip of the king's ground runs down to the water between two dam heads.
You could have said otherwise in there and been believed. I know what that is worth, and I know I cannot pay it in pennies. A count who paid for such things would deserve what came to him.
I burned your stick the day it was closed. I have kept the ash of no other.

This ground is mine to give, for the king. Lie here, build here, and bring me a hen at Michaelmas for it. One hen. I like to be reminded of the day. And my table drinks what your boat brings, at my price, which is a good one.
And take this bolt. It came out of the Avars' ring with the rest of what the king shared among his counts. My wife says it is too good for a hall with dogs in it.
Or sit with the seven who find judgment in my court. A man who knows what a day costs should say what other men's days cost.

The king asked who found the hawk. I said a Frisian who pays on the day. He laughed and said there was no such beast. No layman is free of the tenth at Dorestat, shipman. But there was never such a hawk at Aachen either. Ask, and I will carry the asking.
Take the ground on the king's bank
Ask instead for a seat among the seven who find judgment
Ask him to carry your asking to the king: the freedom of the toll
The count's enemy
The hall is quiet. The king's man has finished with the sticks, and the count has come back in from the door to hear what is said of him at his own board.

It is found. A count may not sell a free man's debt for a gift, nor take back more than he lent. Every bought stick is to be burned, and the count owes the king's ban, sixty shillings. It is written, and I carry the writing.
And you will want this. It says you stand under the lord Charles's word, and that whoever lays a hand on your boat answers to him. Keep it dry.
I find the sticks in order and the count within his right. That is all I find.
He does not look at you as he says it. In the yard a boy is leading one of the count's horses round to the king's man's baggage.
You have made an enemy who holds the toll, the court and the levy of this district, shipman. I hope it was worth an afternoon's talk.
They will say the sticks were mine. They always say the sticks were the steward's.
My lord at Traiectum asks whether you would care to tell him what you told the king's man. He says he has a longer memory, and a storehouse inside stone walls.
Take the king's man's letter and carry for the palace
Take the letter, and ask back twofold what was taken from you
Go down to Traiectum, and trade from behind the bishop's wall
Hands between hands

In the small stone church of Saint Martin, inside the fort at Traiectum, you kneel and put your hands between the bishop's. A clerk writes your name under the names of the saint's other men on the banks at Dorestat.
Now you are Saint Martin's, and he has never yet lost a man to a count.
My clerk goes up to Dorestat with the silver in the morning. The count will take it. He will not like the hand it comes from, and that is between him and me, as everything is.
There is a house-place for you on our bank, by the church above the town. No officer of the king lodges in it, and none takes a tenth of what you sell from it. That is in the kings' own writing.
For this you bring Saint Martin what he asks when he asks it, and you answer in my hall. He asks seldom. I ask oftener.
Ask what Saint Martin wants carried first
Ask that a clerk teach your house its letters
Thiadbod's second boat
The count has ridden east with the host. Your hazel stick hangs in Thiadbod's storehouse now, on a peg between two others, and Thiadbod is pouring the wine himself.
There it hangs, between Sibrad's and a Dane's. I do not call sticks in. A man who owes me rows harder than a man I pay.
You lie at my dam head and carry what I load, and a third of what the boat earns is mine until I say otherwise. For that, no toll man opens your hold, and the count's steward forgets your name.
You have carried for me before. You know I pay.
He said the same to Sibrad, word for word. I will stand witness to the third, if you ask me. Then a third it stays.
Drink with him and sail as his second boat
Ask the widow to stand witness to the terms first
This year there is great hunger in the land of the Franks. Wheat brought up the river to Dorestat before the frost finds a buyer in the count's steward.
The host goes east into Saxony when the grass is up. The count of Dorestat wants hulls at Daventre to carry its stores, from Easter to harvest, and pays a penny a load.

Dawn at a dam head at Dorestat, mist on the river: a thin grey steward in a plain brown cloak, notched sticks at his belt, holds out half of a split hazel stick to a young Frisian skipper standing in a small open boat.

Midday on the plank bank road, bright and windy: a well-fed skipper in a long blue cloak with a silver pin stands over the small boat, smiling, one ringed hand on a wine cask; behind him a woman in a white head-cloth watches from a storehouse door, keys at her belt.

A Michaelmas evening in a timber hall, firelight and smoke: the count in a red cloak sits behind a board, a sword across his knees; the steward fits the two halves of a hazel stick together on the board; the skipper stands before them holding a leather purse.

A grey winter morning on the river bank, thin ice in the ditches: the steward with a wax tablet looks down into the open hold of the small boat; behind him thin people wait at the door of a small wooden church, where a priest stands with empty hands.

Noon inside the mint, a charcoal fire glowing: the moneyer in a leather apron holds up a pair of scales, old pennies in one pan and fewer new ones in the other; the count and the steward watch; a guard stands in the bright doorway.

An early autumn morning in the yard of the hall, light rain, horses saddled: the count, cloaked for the road, points at a hazel stick lying on a trestle beside a purse and a wine cask; the rival in his blue cloak stands at his elbow; the widow watches from the gate.

Late afternoon inside the old stone fort at Traiectum, low sun on pale tuff walls: the bishop in a white alb and dark cloak, ring and plain curled staff, sits on a bench before a small stone church; a deacon holds a book; the skipper stands before him, cap in hand.

A May morning on the river bank at Daventre, wet grass and a clear sky: carts, sacks and horse lines along the water; one of the count's men with a wax tablet counts loads into the small boat; a wooden church stands on a river dune behind.

Evening at the dam head, calm and golden: the count himself bends over a white hawk on a perch in the stern of the small boat as the skipper draws the cloth from her; the steward stands behind with his sticks, forgotten.

A summer day in the count's hall, doors open, dust in the light: a stranger in a travel-worn cloak sits in the count's seat with a clerk writing beside him; tally sticks cover the board; the count stands by the door with folded arms; free men wait in a line to swear.

A Michaelmas morning on the river bank, clear and cold: the count paces out a strip of ground between two dam heads; the steward drives in a hazel peg; the skipper stands by with a live hen under one arm.

Late afternoon in the hall, long shadows: the king's man holds out a folded, sealed leaf to the skipper; the count stands apart by the fire, half turned away; the steward kneels at the hearth, feeding hazel sticks to the flames.

Morning in the small stone church of Saint Martin at Traiectum, light from one narrow window: the skipper kneels with his hands between the bishop's; a clerk writes a name on a parchment roll; a wax candle burns on the altar.

Dusk inside a storehouse on a dam head, a tallow lamp lit and rain at the door: a row of hazel sticks on pegs, one newly hung; the rival pours wine into two cups; the widow stands in the doorway; a gaunt oarsman looks up from a coil of rope.
